paragraphs: The unnamed footway ends here, on asphalt, lit at night. A residential area lies to the west. The path has no name, and seems to manage without one.

Right here there is a platform. It has a bench, a bin and a shelter. There is tactile paving, it takes wheelchairs, and it is lit, like the footway that brought you. It carries a code, 9400ZZCRADD1, which is a name of sorts for whoever needs one.

Beside it runs the tram, “London Trams (Elmers End Branch)”, one way only. Contact line, voltage 750, gauge 1435, maxspeed 80, operated by Transport for London. Its frequency is given as 0. I would not plan a day around that figure. Or I would, and the day would be a long one.
There is more on this platform than I first took in. A bench, a bin, a shelter, the paving, and then something else again, and somewhere after that I have lost the count. The map has not.

Everton Road meets Lower Addiscombe Road here. Asphalt, lit, pavement on both sides, 20 mph. The Addiscombe Village shopping area lies to the north-west, a residential area to the south-east, and the corner seems to belong to both.

Beside you, at 227, there is a cafe, Cafe Adagio, with outdoor seating. There was a cafe with outdoor seating in October 2018. That is when it was last recorded. By another account it sold that November for 10000, which is not much for a cafe, or for whatever was sold. Another account again has the shopfront altered: stall risers, laminated double glazing, open grille shutters, hand written signage. Approved in May 2024. The map has not caught up.
A few steps north, at 229, there is a bookmaker, William Hill. The two shops sit side by side and do not share a postcode. I would not bet on why.
Beyond that there is more, and then more again. I had it counted once. The corner keeps its own count.

Ashburton Road, heading towards Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot. The limit is 20 mph, for what that is worth. This is a residential area, and it reads like one. Nothing much is claimed for it.

A few steps to the south there is a speed hump. It carries a reference, RWG217603, which is more than most things here can say for themselves. Someone thought it worth numbering. The number is longer than the hump.

That is all, or nearly all. I had expected more. I looked again and there was the hump, and the asphalt, and the 20 mph, and then I stopped. There may be something else. I would not like to say what. I would not like to say there is not.

Sundridge Road meets Sundridge Place here. Asphalt, lit at night, pavement on both sides, 20 mph. This is a residential area. The “Addiscombe Village shopping area” starts to the south-east, and one of its premises has come round the corner to stand beside you.
To the west is a building at 1A. It has a number and no name. It was there in July 2013, when it was last recorded. It is there now, so far as the map knows, which is as far as I know.

To the east is 207 Lower Addiscombe Road, CR0 6RB: Brothers Kebab, a fast food place. Kebab, takeaway. It was a takeaway in October 2018. By another account, the Food Standards Agency's, it is a takeaway/sandwich shop, rated 5 in April 2025. The map says nothing of sandwiches. I would not argue with either.
A few steps to the south-west there is another building, with neither name nor number. There was one in July 2013. I have nothing to add, and nor has the map.

Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night. The Addiscombe Village shopping area lies to the north-west, a residential area to the south. The road runs between the two and belongs to neither.

Beside you, at 231, is a cafe, The Tram Stop Cafe. The name promises a tram stop. The map gives me a cafe, which is the half I can vouch for. By another account it holds a hygiene rating of 5, dated 27 October 2025. By another again, its use as a restaurant and cafe, with alterations to the shopfront, was approved on 14 April 2011.
Next door, at 229, is a bookmaker, William Hill. It is a fair place to take your chances, if you came here meaning to.
After that the shopping area carries on, and I begin to count. 231, 229, then the next, and the one after. Somewhere about there I lose the number. The buildings keep theirs.
A footway with no name. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night. A residential area lies to the east. I could not tell you whose.

To the west, beside you, runs the tram line, London Trams (Elmers End Branch). Transport for London operate it. It is electrified by contact line, at a voltage of 750, on a gauge of 1435. One way only. The top speed is given as 80. The frequency is given as 0. Both figures sit in the same record, and I am not the one to reconcile them.
Also to the west, beside you, there is something else: a boundary, political, a ward. It has no name either. The map holds it as firmly as the rails.
So there is the footway, the tram, the boundary, the residential area. That makes four, or five if the contact line counts on its own. Beyond those I begin again, and lose my place. The map does not.
You are at the end of a service. It has no name, or none that was written down. It ends here, and so, for the moment, do you.

There is nothing in particular. I looked for something, I think. A number, a name, a shop that was once a bank. There is not even that. There is the end of the service, and the service behind it, and that is the whole of the inventory.

I hesitate to say more. There is little here. It may be that there was more once, or that there will be, but I have no record of either and will not pretend to one. A service with no name is still a service. It does its work without being called anything.
Addiscombe is somewhere about. I would not stay long.

Everton Road, between Addiscombe Avenue and Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt, lit, pavement on both sides. The limit is 20 mph, which seems generous for a residential area. The Addiscombe Village shopping area lies to the south-east, close enough to count.

A few steps south, at 227 Lower Addiscombe Road, there is a cafe, Cafe Adagio. There was a cafe, with outdoor seating, on the fourth of October 2018. That is when it was last recorded. Croydon, CR0 6RB, should you need to write.
Elsewhere, by another account, the place sold for 10000 on the twentieth of November 2018, some six weeks after the cafe was last recorded. The account gives the figure and no more.

By yet another account, alterations to the shopfront were approved in May 2024: facade redecoration, stall risers, laminated double glazing, a replacement front door, open grille shutters, hand written signage. Whether it is still Cafe Adagio behind the new door, I could not say. The map stops in 2018.

Ashburton Road meets Lower Addiscombe Road here. Asphalt underfoot, 20 mph, for what that is worth. This is Addiscombe: a residential area to the south-east, and to the north-west the “Addiscombe Village shopping area”.
A few steps north-east there is bicycle parking. Stands, with a capacity of 8. Whether all 8 are ever taken at once I could not tell you.

About 30 metres off in the same direction, at 207 Lower Addiscombe Road, is Brothers Kebab, a kebab takeaway. Or it was in October 2018, when it was last recorded. The map has nothing later. By another account it is a takeaway/sandwich shop, rated 5 in April 2025. The two accounts do not quite agree on what it is, and I will not settle it for them.
Beyond that there is more, a good deal more. I begin counting and give up after two. Lower Addiscombe Road, I suspect, keeps its own count.

Sundridge Road comes in here and meets Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt, lit at night, pavement on both sides. The limit is 20 mph, for what that is worth. Houses lie to the south-east; to the north-west, the “Addiscombe Village shopping area”. It is all Addiscombe, whichever way you face.
Beside you, on the south-east side, there are bicycle stands. Room for 8. I make no claim about the bicycles.

A few steps north, at 207, there is a kebab shop, Brothers Kebab. There was a kebab shop in October 2018, when it was last recorded. By another account, a takeaway of that name was rated 5 in April 2025. The map keeps to 2018.

Next to it, at 209–213, a retail building, closed. Its old name is “est Bank”. Or it was NatWest, a bank with an ATM, recorded in October 2018 and gone from the map since January 2021. I am not sure which name is the right one. Beyond that there is more, and I begin to count it, and somewhere along the way I lose the count.

Inglis Road meets Lower Addiscombe Road here. The limit is 20 mph, for what that is worth. Houses lie to the south-east. To the north is the Addiscombe Village shopping area, which is what the map calls it.

A few steps east there is a bus stop. It is called Ashburton Road. You are standing at Inglis Road. I make nothing of that; stops take their names from somewhere. It carries the letters AN and faces west. There is no bench, no shelter and no tactile paving. That is how it was in December 2020, when it was last recorded. It may still be so. It was then.
About 25 metres north-east there is a post box, Royal Mail, CR0 208. It has a number rather than a name, and nobody has called it anything else.
Bingham Road. Asphalt, lit, 20 mph. A residential area lies to the south and keeps to itself.

To the east, close enough to touch, runs the tram: London Trams (Elmers End Branch), operated by Transport for London. One way only. Electrified by contact line, voltage 750. Gauge 1435. A maximum speed of 80, which is a lot to ask of a branch beside a 20 mph road. Frequency, according to the map, 0. I take that as a figure, not a promise. A branch can be named for Elmers End and still keep you waiting.
To the south-east, beside you, is the tram level crossing, where road and tram agree to take turns.

There is more here, I think. The tram, the crossing, the road, the residential area to the south. Then a second something, or the first again from another side. I had the number a moment ago. I have lost it. The crossing has not.
Bingham Road. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night, 20 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south. I know it no better than that.

To the west, beside you, runs the tram: “London Trams (Elmers End Branch)”. Transport for London operates it, one way only. It is electrified by contact line at a voltage of 750, gauge 1435, with a limit of 80. Its frequency is given as 0. A branch with a name, a limit of 80 and a frequency of nothing. I set the two numbers side by side and leave them there.
Beside it, also to the west, is a tram level crossing, where the road and the branch take turns. The road keeps its 20. The tram keeps its 80.
There is more here than that, or there was. I count the line, the crossing, the road, the residential area, and then I lose my place. The map does not.
Ashburton Road, heading towards Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot. The limit is 20 mph, and the road has taken its own steps to see that it is kept.

A few steps to the north there is a speed hump. That is all, or nearly all. It has a reference, RWG217603, which is more than most humps can say for themselves. Someone thought it worth numbering. I have no quarrel with that. A thing with a number is harder to lose.

I had expected more here. I am not sure why. Perhaps there is more and it was never written down, or perhaps there is only the road, the hump and the limit. I would rather say too little than invent the rest.
Go over it slowly. That is what it is for.

Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt, lit at night, 30 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south-east. The Addiscombe Village shopping area lies to the north-west, and you stand at its edge.

Beside you, at 219-221, is Streets Ahead, an estate agent. It was there in October 2018. Next door, at 223-225, is a variety store called Discount Store. There was one that same month, when it was last recorded.

A few steps east, at 5 Bingham Corner, is The Claret. The Claret & Ale, I should say. It was The Claret in January 2017, and I am not sure which is right. It has live sport and toilets for customers. By another account it is the Claret & Ale, rated 4 in July 2021.
West, at 209-213, is a closed retail building, its old name given as “est Bank”. There was a NatWest here, with an ATM. After that I lose count. Two more, perhaps three. The road keeps its own tally.

Lower Addiscombe Road and Bingham Road meet here. Asphalt, lit at night, 30 mph for anyone keeping to it. This is Addiscombe. The Addiscombe Village shopping area keeps to the north-west; a residential area keeps to the south.

Beside you, at 209-213, is a retail building, closed. It was a bank. There was a NatWest here, with an ATM, until January 2021, when it went from the map; it was last recorded in October 2018. Its old name is given as “est Bank”. NatWest, then, or “est Bank”. I would not like to choose.

Next door, at 207, there is a kebab shop, Brothers Kebab, a takeaway. There was one in October 2018, which is when it was last recorded. Elsewhere, by the Food Standards Agency's account, Brothers Kebab is a takeaway/sandwich shop, rated 5 in April 2025. I leave the two accounts to it.
Beyond them there is more, and more after that. I lose count before I am done.

Sundridge Place, between Inglis Road and Sundridge Road. Cobblestone underfoot, which not every street can claim. You are in the Addiscombe Village shopping area, with a residential area to the north-west, near enough to lean on.

Right here there is a building. That is all the map will say of it: a building. There was a building in July 2013, when it was last recorded. I expect there still is. Buildings are reliable in that way, if in no other.

A few steps to the south-east is “Damas Grill/Piri Pirifection/Piri Piri&Co/Lebanese Grill 2”. The map does not have it. By another account, the Food Standards Agency's, it is a takeaway, or a sandwich shop, rated 5 on 6 January 2025. One place, or four. I count the grills, then the piri piris, and lose my place somewhere after the second. The name does not.

Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night, 30 mph, for what that is worth. The Addiscombe Village shopping area lies to the north-west. A residential area lies to the south. You are between the two, which is where most roads put you.

East, beside you, runs the tram: London Trams (Elmers End Branch), operated by Transport for London. One way only. Contact line overhead, voltage 750, gauge 1435. Its maxspeed is 80, which puts the road's 30 in its place. Its frequency is recorded as 0. Either a tram line with no trams, or a number left blank. I would not wait for one. I would not step out in front of one either.
North-east, beside you, a tram level crossing, where road and tram agree to take turns.

After that it gets busy. There is the crossing, the line, the shopping area beyond, then something else, and something after that, and I lose count at three, or perhaps four. The road keeps going regardless.
The footway ends here, unnamed. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night. It has brought you this far without ever saying what it was called. A residential area lies to the east.

Right here is a platform. It has a bench, a bin, a shelter, tactile paving, lighting, and room for a wheelchair. It goes by 9400ZZCRADD2, which is more of a name than the footway managed. I start to count what it holds: the bench, the bin, the shelter, the paving, the lights. Somewhere after that I lose my place, and I let the rest stand.

To the west, beside you, runs the line, "London Trams (Elmers End Branch)". It goes one way only, and Transport for London operates it. Contact line, 750 volts, gauge 1435, top speed 80. Its frequency is given as 0. I would not plan a day around that figure. Nor would I quite dismiss it.

Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt, lit, 30 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south-east. To the north-west is the Addiscombe Village shopping area, which is what it calls itself, and I see no reason to argue.
Beside you, to the west, a post box. Royal Mail, CR0 208. It has a number where another thing might have a name, and the number is all the map gives it.

A few steps north-west, by another account, there is a takeaway and sandwich shop. The map does not have it. The Food Standards Agency has it as “Damas Grill/Piri Pirifection/Piri Piri&Co/Lebanese Grill 2”. Two grills, then the piri piri, then more piri piri, or is it three grills. I lost count somewhere about the Lebanese. The same account gives it a rating of 5, dated 6 January 2025.
After that the shopping area goes on. I started counting and did not finish.
Bingham Road. Asphalt, lit at night, 20 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south.
Beside you, to the south, there is a gate. There was a gate in October 2021, when it was last recorded. Whether it stands open or shut the map does not say, and I would not lean on it either way.

A few steps east runs the tram, “London Trams (Elmers End Branch)”, operated by Transport for London. Contact line, 750 volts. Gauge 1435. One way only. The limit there is 80, a good deal more than the road allows. The frequency is given as 0. A tram with a frequency of 0 still has its name and its voltage, and I leave the rest to the map.
Beyond these there is more, I am fairly sure. I had two, then three, then I was no longer certain what I was counting. The road kept going without me.
Sundridge Road, between Highbarrow Road and Sundridge Place. Asphalt underfoot, pavement on both sides, lit at night. The limit is 20 mph. Few will need telling.

To the south-west, beside you, there is a building. The map says building, and then yes, and that is all it says. It is a building. It was a building in July 2013, when it was last recorded. Whether it is one still, I would not swear to it, though I would be surprised to learn otherwise.

There is little else. I had expected... I am not sure what I had expected. More, perhaps. Sundridge Road lends its name to Sundridge Place, or borrows it, and between the two there is this. I stood here once and could not have told you why. I cannot now.
The footway ends here, without a name, so its end has none either. A residential area lies to the south-west. That is as much as the map allows it.

To the west, beside you, is the tram line, London Trams (Elmers End Branch). Transport for London operates it. It runs one way only, on a gauge of 1435, under a contact line at a voltage of 750 and a frequency of 0. The maximum speed is 80. I would not test it from the footway.
Also to the west, beside you, there is a boundary. It is political: a ward. This map gives the ward no name. The tram got a name, and the line it runs along got a number.

Beyond these there is more. The line, the boundary, the residential area, then something else, and something after that. I had them in order a moment ago. Somewhere between the third and the fourth I lost the count. The map did not.
An unnamed service road, between Bingham Road and a dead end. That is the whole of its route, and it does not pretend otherwise. A residential area, the map says. I am inclined to agree with it.

A few steps to the north-east stands a substation. UK Power Networks operates it, and it carries the number 212167. Minor distribution, by the map's account, which is a modest thing to say of oneself. The service has no name, but the substation has a number, and in this place a number will do.

To the north, a few steps away, there is a gate. There was a gate in October 2021; that is when it was last recorded. Whether it is open or shut I could not tell you now, and I could not have told you then.
Beyond these there is more. One, then two, then the residential area takes over and I lose my place. The dead end, at least, keeps still.

Lower Addiscombe Road, asphalt underfoot, lit at night. The limit is 30 mph, and I would not stake much on it. Addiscombe on all sides: houses to the south-east, and to the north-west the “Addiscombe Village shopping area”.
A few steps east are bicycle stands, room for 8. The map gives them a reference, RWG207888, which is more than most bicycles get.

North, at 207, is Brothers Kebab, a takeaway. There is a kebab shop there; there was one in October 2018, when it was last recorded. Elsewhere, by the Food Standards Agency's account, it is a takeaway/sandwich shop, rated 5 in April 2025. The two accounts are seven years apart. I leave them so.
North-east, at 209–213, stands a retail building, closed. There was a bank here. Its old name is recorded as “est Bank”. The address has outlasted the bank. Addresses usually do.

Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt, lit at night, 30 mph, which is a figure rather than a promise. Houses lie to the south-east. To the north-west is the retail side, “Addiscombe Village shopping area”, and it is all Addiscombe whichever way you face.
A few steps east there is bicycle parking. It asks nothing of you and offers about the same.

North, at 207, is Brothers Kebab, a fast food place. Kebab, takeaway. There is a kebab shop here; there was one in October 2018, when it was last recorded. By another account it was given a food hygiene rating of 5 in April 2025, which would put it here well after the map last had it. I would not stake much either way.
North-east, 209-213 is a retail building. It was a bank once, “est Bank”. The bank has gone, and the numbers 209-213 remain.

Everton Road, between Addiscombe Avenue and Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night, pavement on both sides. The limit is 20 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area, with the “Addiscombe Village shopping area” off to the south-east. This is a road to be on the way to somewhere.

A few steps south, at 227 Lower Addiscombe Road, there is a cafe, “Cafe Adagio”, with outdoor seating. There was a cafe with outdoor seating in October 2018, when it was last recorded. I would not wager against it now.

By another account it sold for £10,000 in November 2018, a month after the map last had it. By another, an application was approved in May 2024: facade redecoration, stall risers, laminated double glazing, a replacement front door, open grille shutters, and hand written signage. The map knows nothing of either. The signage, if it went up, was written by hand.
You are on Bingham Road. Asphalt, lit at night, 20 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south. It keeps to itself, as such areas do.

To the west, beside you, runs the tram. The map calls it “London Trams (Elmers End Branch)”, run by Transport for London. A branch, then, and one that tells you where it ends before you have set foot on it. I have known less honest arrangements.
There is a tram level crossing here too, on the same side. Road and rail share the ground and take turns. The tram does not wait for opinions.
There is more about, and I will let it go. The crossing is the thing to mind. Look both ways along the Elmers End Branch before you step onto it.

Sundridge Road meets Lower Addiscombe Road here. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night, pavement on both sides. The limit is 20 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south-east, and the Addiscombe Village shopping area to the north-west. There is more here than I will set down.
Beside you, to the south-east, there is bicycle parking. Useful, if you came on one.

A few steps north, at 207, there is a fast food place, Brothers Kebab. Kebab, takeaway. There was a kebab shop there in October 2018, when it was last recorded. By another account, the Food Standards Agency's, its food hygiene rating is 5, given in April 2025.

Next door, 209–213 is a retail building. It was a bank. There was a NatWest at this address, gone from the map since January 2021. Or it was “est Bank”. I have it under both names and could not tell you which is right. Either way the bank has gone, and 209–213 Lower Addiscombe Road is still there.

Sundridge Road, between Highbarrow Road and Sundridge Place. Asphalt underfoot, pavement on both sides, lit at night. The limit is 20 mph, for what that is worth. I have never been sure what it is worth.
Beside you, to the south-west, there is a building. The map calls it a building and says no more. It is the plainest word the map has, and the map chose it.

There was a building there in July 2013. That is when it was last recorded. There is one now, I should think, or there was then, and nothing since has said otherwise. I take the map at its word. It is the only word I have been given.
The road has a name, and the place at its end borrows it. The building beside you has none. Sundridge Place lies at one end of this stretch, Highbarrow Road at the other.

Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night, a limit of 30 mph, for what that is worth. To the north-west lies the Addiscombe Village shopping area, a retail area by the map's reckoning and a village by its own. To the south is a residential area, and the map says no more of it than that.
Beside you to the east runs the tram, “London Trams (Elmers End Branch)”. It is named for Elmers End, which is somewhere else. Transport for London runs it. I have no quarrel with either arrangement.

Beside you to the north-east is a tram level crossing, where the line and the road agree to share. Other things press in around it, and I let them go by. The crossing is the part worth knowing, and it is here, on Lower Addiscombe Road, with the tram on one side of you and the asphalt under your feet.
Bingham Road. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night, and a limit of 20 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south. You are beside it, not in it.
Nearest, on the south side, there is a gate. There was a gate in October 2021, which is when it was last recorded. It may still open. It may never have been asked to. The map keeps it all the same.
A few steps east is the tram, “London Trams (Elmers End Branch)”. Transport for London runs it. The name is longer than the road it crosses, and more particular about where it belongs.
There is more along Bingham Road, and I will let it go. The gate is south of you, and to the east, the tram that Transport for London runs.

Ashburton Road comes in here and meets Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot, and a limit of 20 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south-east. To the north-west is the “Addiscombe Village shopping area”, which is a retail area, whatever else the name hopes for.
A few steps to the north-east there is bicycle parking. The map says no more about it than that, and I see no reason to improve on the map.
There is a good deal close by. I began counting it and lost my place somewhere after the bicycle parking. No matter. I carry on.

About 30 metres north-east, at 207 Lower Addiscombe Road, is Brothers Kebab, a fast food place. It serves kebab, takeaway. It served kebab in October 2018, at any rate, which is when it was last recorded. By another account, its food hygiene rating is 5, given in April 2025.

Lower Addiscombe Road, asphalt underfoot, lit at night. The Addiscombe Village shopping area lies to the north-west, a residential area to the south. You stand between the two, which is as good a place as any.

Beside you, at 231, is a cafe, “The Tram Stop Cafe”. The map calls it a cafe and says no more. By another account, an application was made in April 2011 for use as a restaurant and cafe, with alterations to the shopfront, and it was approved. When the name arrived, I cannot say.
Next door, at 229, is a bookmaker, William Hill. Beyond these two the shops go on, and I let them go.
Elsewhere, the cafe was given a food hygiene rating of 5 in October 2025. Between the bookmaker and the cafe, I would choose the cafe. A 5 is a 5.

Sundridge Road meets Sundridge Place here. Asphalt, lit at night, pavement on both sides, 20 mph. Sundridge twice over, a road and a place. The area is residential, with the “Addiscombe Village shopping area” just to the south-east.

To the west, beside you, is a building at 1A. There was a building at 1A in July 2013, when it was last recorded. The map gives it an address and nothing more. A few steps to the south-west is another building, without even that, also last recorded in July 2013.

To the east, beside you, is Brothers Kebab, at 207 Lower Addiscombe Road. It serves kebab. Takeaway. So it was in October 2018, when it was last recorded. By another account, the Food Standards Agency's, it has a food hygiene rating of 5, given in April 2025. The map stops in 2018. The other account carries on to 2025. Brothers Kebab, either way.
The footway ends here. It has no name, or none the map will give it. A residential area lies to the south-west, and you are beside it rather than in it.

To the west, close at hand, is a tram: “London Trams (Elmers End Branch)”. Run by Transport for London, the map says. It is a long name for something so near, and it carries an End in it, which is more than the footway has managed. I hold that opinion lightly.

Also to the west, also beside you, there is something. The map says only that: something. I had the tram, then the something, and somewhere between the two I lost count. I take it up again where I left it. The footway still has no name. The tram still belongs to Transport for London, and still to the Elmers End Branch.

Sundridge Place, between Inglis Road and Sundridge Road. Cobblestone underfoot, which is worth knowing before you hurry. This is the Addiscombe Village shopping area, so the map says, with a residential area to the north-west.
Right here there is a building. There was a building in July 2013, when it was last recorded. The map gives it no name and no purpose. I will not supply either.

A few steps to the south-east is “Damas Grill/Piri Pirifection/Piri Piri&Co/Lebanese Grill 2”. The map does not have it. By another account, the Food Standards Agency's, its food hygiene rating is 5, given in January 2025.

I had counted one, then two, then somewhere among the grills I lost count. I carried on regardless. The map keeps its building here, as it was in July 2013. The other account keeps a grill a few steps south-east, rated 5.

You are on a service with no name, running between Bingham Road and a dead end. This is a residential area. The service makes no claim to be more than it is, and one end of it, by the map's own account, leads nowhere at all.

A few steps to the north-east there is a substation, run by UK Power Networks. It carries a reference, “212167”. So the substation has a reference and the service has none. That seems the wrong way round, but nobody asked me.
There is more close in behind these, and I let it go.

A few steps to the north there is a gate. There was a gate in October 2021, when it was last recorded. I would expect it is still there. Gates tend to stay put, open or shut, long after anyone has written them down.

Lower Addiscombe Road. Asphalt underfoot, lit at night, a limit of 30 mph, for what that is worth. A residential area lies to the south-east. To the north-west is the “Addiscombe Village shopping area”, and it is busy. I take the nearest of it and let the rest go by.
